/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.headline: Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.excerpt: Cancer diagnoses in England have hit record highs, with more than 1,000 people a day diagnosed, NHS figures show. But experts warned that although the health service was identifying more cases, it was still failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment. According to the latest cancer registration statistics, more than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest figure on record. On average, NHS England diagnosed 1,021 people a day with cancer in 2024, up from 972 a day in 2023. Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers accounted for half of all new diagnoses. The figures showed improvements in stage at diagnosis: 56.7% of first new cancers were diagnosed at stage 1 and 2 in 2024 compared with 55.8% in 2023. Prof Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, said the figures showed the health service was “moving in the right direction” and were testimony to NHS staff’s hard work. He said: “NHS teams across the country are taking tests and checks closer to the people who need them, and with new treatments being developed all the time, we will continue to do all we can to get people seen and treated for cancer as early as possible.” Experts urged caution, however, given the NHS is failing to meet its timescale targets. The latest monthly NHS figures show that 78.6% of patients in England urgently referred for suspected cancer were diagnosed or had cancer ruled out within 28 days in August – below the target of 80%.
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.trail: While NHS is identifying more cases, it is failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment, experts say

/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.headline: Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.excerpt: People from minority ethnic backgrounds in England are up to a third less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via routine screening, and are more likely to be diagnosed in an emergency setting, analysis has found. The research, carried out by academics at the University of Surrey and funded by the charity Breast Cancer Now, involved analysis of 86,564 adults diagnosed with the disease between 2009 and 2019, from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and the Cancer Registration Tumour and Treatment datasets. The analysis found that people from Black, Asian and mixed backgrounds, alongside people from deprived backgrounds, were up to 33% less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, while these groups were also up to 31% more likely to be diagnosed via urgent suspected cancer referral, and up to 37% more likely to be diagnosed via emergency presentation. Manveet Basra, the associate director of public health, inclusion and awareness at Breast Cancer Now, said the analysis revealed that people from marginalised groups “face inequalities at every stage of their breast cancer experience, and tragically this impacts their survival rates”. Basra added: “This research helps us understand who is less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, [who] might wait longer to get diagnosed or experience delays in treatment, and knowing what barriers they face enables us to work towards eliminating them.

/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.headline: Woman told she had cancer by NHS worker who inappropriately accessed her records
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.excerpt: A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee she barely knew who had accessed her medical records days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant. Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall hospital in Truro. Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said her personal information was accessed by a man she knew only vaguely who worked at the hospital. She said: “I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. This man said to me: ‘Pippa, I don’t want you to worry, but you’ve got cancer.’ I just couldn’t really believe it.” Two days later, Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer. Boardman, who is recovering well from the cancer, said Royal Cornwall’s handling of the case had reinforced her trauma, and she said the trust only apologised once it had been contacted by reporters at the BBC. She told the BBC: “It really distresses me people can’t see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately.” A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said: “We are truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way. Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her and discuss her diagnosis. This should not have happened, and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.

/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.headline: UK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopause
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.excerpt: Doctors have developed a simple test that could help rule out womb cancer in women who experience bleeding after menopause. The approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women each year and spare them from invasive and uncomfortable tests that can also be costly for healthcare systems. Every year, hundreds of thousands of women worldwide are diagnosed with womb cancer. Bleeding after menopause triggers an urgent cancer referral but only about 5% to 10% of women who report bleeding have an underlying cancer. Currently, the tests for womb cancer – an internal ultrasound scan, a biopsy of the womb lining and hysteroscopy, in which a camera is passed into the womb – are all invasive and costly. The new test, developed at the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, looks at cells collected from the urine and vaginal fluid. It is cheap and non-invasive. In a study assessing the test, 1,864 women attending seven hospitals in north-west England with postmenopausal bleeding gave a urine sample and a vaginal fluid sample before their routine tests. Of these women, 5% (99 of the 1,864) were diagnosed with womb cancer via a biopsy or surgery. Using the new test, cytologists unaware of the women’s diagnoses identified 80 of the 99 womb cancers and correctly returned a negative result for 93% of women who did not have womb cancer. The findings were published in the journal Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women’s Health.
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.trail: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies

/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.headline: ‘Early deaths are not inevitable’: report reveals why adults with severe mental illness die younger
/society/2026/nov/14/nhs-england-62-day-.excerpt: An analysis of NHS data has shed light on the “scandal” of why adults with severe mental illness are more likely to die 15 to 20 years younger than the general population. The Rethink Mental Illness charity has revealed that adults under 75 with serious mental ill health – defined as those referred to specialist secondary mental health services – are 6.3 times as likely to die from liver disease, 6 times more likely from respiratory illness, 3.8 times more likely from cardiovascular disease and 2.3 times as likely from cancer. They are also 14.6 times as likely to die due to suicide, compared with those who were not referred. Overall, they are 4.8 times more likely to die of any cause before the age of 75 than the general population. For some conditions, these health inequalities are the starkest to date. For working-age adults living with a mental illness, the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are at their highest levels since records began, each with more than 24,000 deaths in the 2022-2024 reporting period, the charity calculated. Cancer, cardiovascular disease, liver disease and respiratory disease accounted for more than half (56.5%) of deaths for 18- to 74-year-olds with severe mental health problems in England during this period. Cancer and cardiovascular disease each accounted for just under 19% of all deaths, respiratory disease 11%, and liver disease 8%. During the same period, suicide comprised 7% of these early deaths.

/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.excerpt: Thick fog will shroud much of the southern half of England, the eastern half of Wales and most of Northern Ireland throughout the early part of the week, forecasters have said, as commuters are told to expect delays. There was disruption to flights at Heathrow airport on Monday, while an incident involving 30 vehicles closed a major road in Kent on Saturday evening. Niamh Murray, a Met Office operational meteorologist, said current weather conditions were the “perfect recipe” for fog. “With autumn and winter … we get much longer nights, and that allows temperatures to fall away,” she said. “We get a longer period of cooling and also the temperatures are much lower, so they’re much closer to the temperature that we need for the air to become saturated and therefore form fog. “Another thing that we need to form fog is quite light winds, not absolutely no winds. We just have the perfect recipe at the moment – light winds, clear skies, long nights – to allow that fog to develop. And particularly if we see the negative numbers [the temperature in degrees celsius], it can be quite stubborn to clear the next day.” Forecasters issued yellow weather warnings, the least severe, for Monday in areas covering: most of England south of Manchester, with the exception of Devon and Cornwall; eastern parts of Wales, including Cardiff; and most of Northern Ireland, with the exception of Belfast.
/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.trail: Drivers warned to take care as ‘perfect’ weather conditions for mist affect areas of England, Wales and Northern Ireland

/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.headline: ‘Everything is so out of whack’: UK trees experience spring six months early
/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.excerpt: Trees are experiencing an “early spring” because of mild UK temperatures this autumn, with experts warning this could cause long-term harm to pollinators. Last month was warmer than average across all parts of the UK, with October marking the ninth consecutive month with above-average mean temperatures. Chris Nichols, the head of conservation outcomes at the Woodland Trust, said the mild weather this autumn meant horse chestnut trees were flowering and showing signs of next year’s spring growth more than six months early. During the extreme heat this summer, many trees underwent “early autumn”, where they wilted and lost their leaves prematurely. Experts said England’s ancient oak trees were dying as a result of high temperatures and drought, as trees and ecosystems struggle to adapt fast enough to the changing climate. Scientists have said the higher than average temperatures are only possible due to the climate crisis, primarily driven by the burning of fossil fuels. “It’s crazy, everything is so out of whack,” Nichols said, adding that the early spring was particularly concerning for pollinators. “Trees need to flower at a certain time of year so they’re in sync with the insects. It’s like an ecological mismatch and it’s concerning in terms of the resilience of trees in the long term if they’re out of whack with the other species that they rely on,” he said.

/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.headline: Major clean-up under way after two storms cause havoc in Britain
/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.excerpt: A major clean-up operation was under way on Monday after weekend storms caused havoc, with forecasters warning of more strong winds to come. Two men were killed by falling trees after two named storms, Austen and Boelo, struck parts of the UK, and there was widespread travel disruption, flooding, power cuts and event cancellations. The Energy Networks Association, which represents operators in the UK and Ireland, said 90,000 customers were still without power on Monday morning. That figure was later down to 39,000. The association’s chief executive, Lawrence Slade, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that disruption had been widespread, with operators having to restore power to about 700,000 customers over the weekend. He said Friday, Saturday and Sunday had been particularly challenging. “It certainly was a tough one. One of the problems was how quickly Boelo followed after Austen,” he said. Another issue was that there was no letup in the strong winds, widely 50-70mph and up to 85mph in northern Scotland. “Until that weather system passes we can’t safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up etc,” Slade said. The weather was much milder on Monday but the Met Office said more strong winds were on the way and issued two yellow weather warnings. One is in place from 6pm until 3am on Tuesday, covering western coastal areas from Cornwall up to south-west Scotland. Gusts of up to 65mph could hit exposed coastal areas, accompanied by heavy rain at times.
/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.trail: More strong winds forecast after Austen and Boelo kill two people and bring travel disruption and flooding

/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.headline: Two dead and tens of thousands of properties without power as Storm Boelo batters UK
/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.excerpt: Two people were killed and more than 800,000 properties left without power after Storm Boelo and Storm Austen battered the UK over the weekend. Two men, one aged 60 and the other in his 20s, were killed by falling trees on Sunday, police said. The 60-year-old died in south-west Scotland while the man in his 20s was killed in London. A spokesperson for Police Scotland said: “We were made aware of a 60-year-old man having been struck by a falling tree on a minor road at Mid Kelton at about 10.30am on Sunday, 25 October 2026. “The man was pronounced dead at the scene. There are no suspicious circumstances and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal in due course.” In London, the man was killed when a tree fell on to his car at 12.40pm as he drove through Mill Hill in the north of the city. Ch Insp Guy Ellwood said: “Our thoughts are with the loved ones of the young man who lost his life.” Storm Boelo arrived in northern parts of the UK on Saturday evening and was the second named storm in as many days, after Storm Austen brought strong winds to south-west England on Friday. The Met Office said wind speeds widely reached 60-70mph, affecting areas in an amber warning zone that came into force at 9pm on Saturday. The warning covered Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, with gusts reaching more than 80mph in exposed coastal spots.
/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-w.trail: Man aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mph

/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.headline: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.excerpt: This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad. In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, completely took over my life. It took the air out of every room – I couldn’t talk about anything else. People stopped commissioning me because they assumed I was busy going to space; every conversation I had was about it. This was going to be the rest of my life. That day in April was pivotal. We were there to watch SpaceX’s Integrated Flight Test 1. After four minutes, following a relatively successful liftoff, the vehicle experienced what they call in space terms an “RUD” – Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly – and broke apart in the air.
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.trail: ‘I was chosen to go around the Moon on a SpaceX starship. Preparations took over my life. Then, four minutes into watching a rocket on a test flight, it broke apart. And that was the end of my adventure’

/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.headline: US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.excerpt: The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor. The access also raises new national security questions, industry observers say. The move comes after Musk’s Doge in 2025 fired many of the federal government’s nascent space traffic control program’s staff, and the administration has twice attempted to financially gut the department, called the Traffic Coordination System for Space (Traccs). The moves were widely viewed in the industry as an attempt by Musk to privatize space traffic control. The defense department has now granted SpaceX access to its most precise data on potential collisions among satellites and other space objects, which will give Musk’s companies an advantage over competition that offers a similar service. SpaceX and the Space Force signed the new contract. The commercial US space market is expected to grow to a value of nearly $2tn in value over the next decade, and the unprecedented access to military data appears to be another step toward Musk asserting monopoly control over commercial space activity more broadly, said Cole Donovan, a former Traccs employee now with the Stand Up for Science non-profit. “It’s making a company the de facto source for space traffic coordination within the US,” Donovan added.
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.trail: This gives the company an advantage in tracking objects in orbit, raising national security concerns and fears of greater control over the space industry

/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.headline: SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.excerpt: A SpaceX rocket provided a stunning pre-dawn display over Florida as a egiant, luminescent “jellyfish cloud” spread for miles, caused by an expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalizing in the sky and reflecting sunlight off the frozen particles. The phenomenon occurred shortly after Tuesday’s 6.33am ET launch of the Falcon 9 rocket carrying cargo to the International Space Station. The timing of the blastoff, 48 minutes before sunrise at Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station, provided a perfect example of the colorful effect only fully visible from Earth during dusk and dawn launches. The rocket’s north-eastern trajectory over the Atlantic also allowed residents of eastern states from Georgia to New York to enjoy the spectacle. Nasa posted photographs of the jellyfish cloud on X, the social media platform owned by the SpaceX chief executive, Elon Musk. Among the hundreds of replies were images taken by sky watchers across multiple states. Those who missed Tuesday’s dazzling celestial show have another opportunity to view one next Monday, 19 October, when another SpaceX Falcon 9 is scheduled to lift off from the same space force station pad. An hour-long launch window for the satellite-deployment mission opens at 6.30am ET, little more than a half-hour before the 7.01am sunrise.
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.trail: Expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalized in the sky and reflected sunlight off frozen particles after Florida launch

/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.headline: ‘Starship is in orbit’: cheers go up as huge SpaceX rocket circles Earth for first time
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.excerpt: SpaceX has sent its enormous Starship rocket into Earth’s orbit for the first time on a milestone flight intended to pave the way for future missions to the moon and Mars. The rocket, the largest and most powerful ever built, blasted off from SpaceX’s Starbase launch facility in Texas at 7.48am local time (1.48pm BST), marking its 14th test flight and first attempt to circle the planet before falling back to Earth. Despite an engine failure on ascent that threatened to prevent Starship from reaching orbit, mission controllers decided it was safe to press ahead with a burn that pushed the ship on to a planned trajectory to take it around the planet. Cheers and applause broke out at SpaceX after initial suggestions that the orbit attempt might be abandoned were quashed and the decision to go ahead was announced. Moments after the orbit burn, Daniel Hewitt, an engineer who was narrating a live stream of the launch, declared: “Starship is in orbit.” Elon Musk’s company has flown Starship in its full form since 2023 but previous test flights have only sought to put the rocket into suborbital trajectories, which are simpler and carry fewer risks for the public. For suborbital flights, the trajectory is such that if the rocket explodes or malfunctions mid-flight, the remnants come down in the Indian Ocean far from populated areas. The risks are harder to control when rockets are on full orbital paths around the planet.
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.trail: Mission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attempt

/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.headline: The US air force admitted to deploying weapons in space. Don’t expect the White House to explain why
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.excerpt: In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good guys, from Captain Kirk and his crew in Star Trek, to Luke Skywalker’s rebel alliance in Star Wars, battle intergalactic villains with an array of colorful lasers and particle-beam cannons, then the bad guys get dispatched in a spectacular, explosive finale. The messaging coming out of the White House on the subject, by contrast, could not be more vague. This week’s attention-grabbing revelation by air force secretary Troy Meink – that the US has deployed some kind of weapons in space – carried nothing in the way of context or detail, and left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal. And, equally importantly, what he intends to do with it. “You can count the words, and the disclosure, on one hand, so there’s not much there to work with, and we really don’t know what kind of weapons he was talking about,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the aerospace security project and a senior fellow in the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said of Meink’s announcement. “The US is looking for another tool to deter what it sees as concerning Russian and Chinese behaviors in space, so my guess is that revealing it has on-orbit weapons would be your way to do that. “[But] that level of detail needed to make this disclosure effective as a deterrent isn’t there.
/science/2026/nov/14/spacex-starship-dou.trail: The revelation ‘left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal’
